subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient has bilateral loss of smell following a head injury. The affected cranial nerve is unique among the twelve in that its fibers reach the cortex without first synapsing in the thalamus.
question: Which cranial nerve is the only one that reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay?

options.text: Optic nerve (CN II)
Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
Olfactory nerve (CN I)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Vagus nerve (CN X)

explanation_correct: The olfactory nerve (CN I) is the only cranial nerve that projects to the cortex without a relay in the thalamus; olfactory fibers synapse in the olfactory bulb and project directly to piriform cortex and associated limbic areas. This distinctive feature explains why smell can be affected by lesions along the olfactory tract and why it is uniquely wired compared with other sensory modalities.

explanation_incorrect.A: CN II (sight) does relay through the thalamus, specifically the lateral geniculate nucleus, on its way to the visual cortex.
explanation_incorrect.B: CN III is primarily a motor nerve to extraocular muscles and the pupil; the no-thalamic-relay distinction belongs to CN I.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN VII carries taste and motor fibers, and taste pathways do relay through the thalamus (VPM nucleus) before reaching cortex.
explanation_incorrect.E: CN X carries visceral sensory and motor fibers and is not the unique nerve that bypasses the thalamus.

educationalObjective: CN I (olfactory) is the only cranial nerve that reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with a compressive oculomotor nerve palsy has a dilated, poorly reactive pupil, ptosis, and an eye resting 'down and out.' The involved nerve normally supplies most extraocular muscles, the sphincter pupillae, the ciliary muscle, and the levator palpebrae superioris.
question: Which of the following is a function of the oculomotor nerve (CN III)?

options.text: Pupillary constriction and accommodation
Abduction of the eye
Elevation of the ipsilateral shoulder
Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
General sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue

explanation_correct: CN III innervates the superior, inferior, and medial recti and the inferior oblique, plus the sphincter pupillae for pupillary constriction, the ciliary muscle for accommodation, and the levator palpebrae for eyelid opening. A palsy therefore produces a dilated pupil, ptosis, and an eye displaced down and out by the unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique.

explanation_incorrect.B: Abduction of the eye is carried out by the lateral rectus, which is innervated by CN VI, not CN III.
explanation_incorrect.C: Shoulder elevation via the trapezius is a function of CN XI.
explanation_incorrect.D: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels with CN VII through the chorda tympani.
explanation_incorrect.E: General sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of CN V.

educationalObjective: CN III controls most eye movements, pupillary constriction, accommodation, and eyelid opening.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient has difficulty looking downward and inward, especially when descending stairs. The affected muscle is the only extraocular muscle supplied by its nerve, and because that nerve decussates, a lesion on one side produces a functional deficit referable to the opposite side.
question: Which of the following statements about the trochlear nerve (CN IV) is correct?

options.text: It innervates the lateral rectus and is the only cranial nerve that decussates.
It arises from the pons and supplies the contralateral superior oblique.
It controls the medial rectus, the only muscle it supplies.
It provides parasympathetic fibers to the sphincter pupillae.
It innervates only the superior oblique and is the only cranial nerve with contralateral function because it crosses the midline.

explanation_correct: CN IV supplies only the superior oblique muscle, which depress and intorts the eye. It is the only cranial nerve that arises dorsally and decussates completely, so each trochlear nerve innervates the contralateral superior oblique—the basis of its 'contralateral function.' Damage produces difficulty with downward-inward gaze, as when walking down stairs.

explanation_incorrect.A: CN IV innervates the superior oblique, not the lateral rectus; the lateral rectus is supplied by CN VI, although CN IV does decussate.
explanation_incorrect.B: CN IV arises from the dorsal midbrain, not the pons, even though it does supply the contralateral superior oblique after decussating.
explanation_incorrect.C: The medial rectus is innervated by CN III, not CN IV; CN IV's sole muscle is the superior oblique.
explanation_incorrect.D: Parasympathetic fibers to the sphincter pupillae travel with CN III, not CN IV.

educationalObjective: CN IV innervates only the superior oblique and is the only cranial nerve that decussates, giving it contralateral function.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with a lesion near the internal auditory meatus has ipsilateral facial weakness, inability to close the eye, sensitivity to loud sounds, decreased lacrimation, and loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. All these findings are explained by involvement of a single cranial nerve.
question: Which of the following is a function of the facial nerve (CN VII)?

options.text: Mastication and general sensation over the face
Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani
Taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue
Hearing and balance
Elevation of the soft palate

explanation_correct: CN VII carries taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue through the chorda tympani, in addition to motor fibers to muscles of facial expression, orbicularis oculi, and stapedius, and parasympathetic fibers for lacrimation and salivation. Hyperacusis reflects stapedius palsy, and reduced lacrimation and anterior tongue taste loss localize the lesion proximal to the chorda tympani branch.

explanation_incorrect.A: Mastication and general facial sensation are functions of CN V (trigeminal), not CN VII.
explanation_incorrect.C: Taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue is carried by CN IX (glossopharyngeal).
explanation_incorrect.D: Hearing and balance are mediated by CN VIII (vestibulocochlear), which runs alongside CN VII in the internal auditory meatus.
explanation_incorrect.E: Elevation of the soft palate is mediated primarily by CN X through the nucleus ambiguus.

educationalObjective: CN VII supplies facial movement, orbicularis oculi, stapedius, anterior two-thirds tongue taste via the chorda tympani, lacrimation, and salivation.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient has loss of taste over the posterior third of the tongue, reduced parotid salivation, and an absent gag reflex after a skull-base lesion. A separate finding of uvular deviation and a diminished cough reflex indicates involvement of the adjacent nerve as well.
question: Which of the following functions is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) but not by the vagus nerve (CN X)?

options.text: Taste from the supraglottic region
Parasympathetic supply to thoracoabdominal viscera
Elevation of the soft palate with a midline uvula
Monitoring carotid body and carotid sinus chemo- and baroreceptors
Branchial motor supply to pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles via the nucleus ambiguus

explanation_correct: CN IX monitors the chemo- and baroreceptors of the carotid body and carotid sinus and supplies taste and sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, the parotid gland, and the stylopharyngeus muscle. CN X instead monitors the aortic arch chemoreceptors and baroreceptors. This distinction makes carotid sinus monitoring the function unique to CN IX among the choices.

explanation_incorrect.A: Supraglottic taste is a function of CN X, not CN IX, so this does not distinguish CN IX from the vagus.
explanation_incorrect.B: Parasympathetic outflow to thoracoabdominal viscera is carried by CN X through its dorsal motor nucleus, not by CN IX.
explanation_incorrect.C: Soft palate elevation with a midline uvula is mediated by CN X; a vagal lesion causes the uvula to deviate away from the side of the lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Branchial motor fibers to pharynx and larynx arise from the nucleus ambiguus shared by CN IX and X, so this is not unique to CN IX.

educationalObjective: CN IX uniquely monitors carotid body and sinus receptors and serves the posterior third of the tongue and parotid gland, whereas CN X serves the aortic arch and thoracoabdominal viscera.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient has marked difficulty turning the head to the right and shrugging the right shoulder after a lesion, but the tongue protrudes in the midline without fasciculations. A second patient demonstrates tongue deviation toward the side of a lesion on protrusion.
question: Which of the following is a function of the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)?

options.text: Tongue protrusion
Elevation of the soft palate
Head turning and shoulder shrugging via sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
Facial expression
Swallowing with taste from the posterior third of the tongue

explanation_correct: CN XI is a motor nerve supplying the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, which turn the head to the opposite side and elevate the shoulder, respectively. Its spinal root ascends through the foramen magnum before joining the cranial root and exiting through the jugular foramen. Tongue movement, by contrast, is the function of CN XII.

explanation_incorrect.A: Tongue protrusion and movement are functions of CN XII (hypoglossal); an injured hypoglossal nerve causes the tongue to deviate toward the lesion.
explanation_incorrect.B: Elevation of the soft palate is mediated by CN X via the nucleus ambiguus.
explanation_incorrect.D: Facial expression is mediated by CN VII (facial nerve).
explanation_incorrect.E: Swallowing with posterior-third tongue taste is mediated by CN IX, with CN X contributing to the motor phase.

educationalObjective: CN XI supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius for head turning and shoulder shrugging, whereas CN XII controls tongue movement.
